candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest predicts MALWARE with probability 0.91, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking. However, the evidence is weak on its own. SHAP contributions are small and almost flat, from +0.0071 (LEA PUSH) to +0.0114 (INC PUSH), so no single feature dominates and the score looks like many weak signals adding up. Most of the n-grams are generic stack and call-convention patterns: CALL PUSH, PUSH CALL, MOV PUSH, SUB PUSH, ADD PUSH, LEA PUSH, POP PUSH, POP CALL, MOV LEAVE and CALL RET. Compiler-generated code commonly contains these, and they are not specific to mining. The most frequent ones (PUSH CALL at 0.0465, MOV PUSH at 0.0403, CALL PUSH at 0.0316, LEA PUSH at 0.0181) suggest a call-heavy, stack-argument-passing code style, which is consistent with many ordinary programs. The rare n-grams (POP SUB at 0.00005, PUSH RET at 0.000017, SBB INC at 0.000033, SHL NEG at 0.000017, POP XOR at 0.000266) have high SHAP weight despite very low frequency. They could reflect unusual or hand-written code, packing or obfuscation, or arithmetic and bit manipulation, but they are too sparse to confirm hashing loops. The evidence lists no function names or locations, no sustained rotate/XOR/shift sequences, and no other mining-specific structure. The model's statistical lean toward malware is real, but the assembly-level evidence cannot confirm cryptojacking specifically, so the classification is inconclusive.
